screens.title: Spot the problem
screens.text: The root of this tree has balance factor 0: its left and right branches have the same height. Is every node balanced?
screens.reveal: No. Nodes 30 and 70 each have one branch two levels taller than the other. Checking only the root is not enough.

screens.title: Goal
screens.text: Calculate heights and balance factors, and decide whether a tree is an AVL tree (LO2).

task.stem: What is the height of a leaf?
task.hint: This checks heights and balance factors: height counts edges down to a leaf, and bf = h(right) − h(left), with an empty branch counted as −1.

options.explanation: That counts the leaf itself as a node. Height counts edges, so a leaf has height 0.
Right. A leaf has no edges below it, so its height is 0.
−1 is the height of an empty branch, one level below a leaf.

screens.title: Height
screens.text: The height of a node is the number of edges on the longest path from the node down to a leaf. A leaf has height 0. An empty branch has height −1, one less than a leaf.
screens.caption: 10, 30 and 50 are leaves (height 0). 40 has height 1. The root 20 has height 2.

screens.title: Balance factor
screens.text: The balance factor of a node is bf = h(right) − h(left).
points: Positive: the right branch is taller.
Negative: the left branch is taller.
0: both branches have the same height.
Node 20: its right branch has height 1 and its left branch has height 0, so bf = 1 − 0 = +1.
Node 10: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch is empty (height −1), so bf = −1 − (−1) = 0.
screens.showRule: bf = height of right branch − height of left branch. An empty branch has height −1.

screens.title: The AVL rule
points: In an AVL tree, every node has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.
The rule applies at every node, not just the root. Every subtree of an AVL tree is itself an AVL tree.
The tree does not have to be perfectly balanced: a difference of 1 is allowed.
Each node stores its height, so balance factors are quick to recompute.
Stated without proof: the height of an AVL tree is at most roughly 1.44 log(n + 2) − 1.328, and in practice only slightly more than log n.
screens.showRule: AVL tree: a BST in which every node has bf −1, 0 or +1.

screens.title: Worked example: from the leaves up
screens.text: Work from the leaves up, because a node’s height depends on its children’s heights.
steps: Node 5: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch is empty (height −1), so bf = −1 − (−1) = 0.
Node 10: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch has height 0, so bf = −1 − 0 = −1.
Node 25: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch is empty (height −1), so bf = −1 − (−1) = 0.
Node 20: its right branch has height 0 and its left branch has height 1, so bf = 0 − 1 = −1.
Node 50: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch is empty (height −1), so bf = −1 − (−1) = 0.
Node 40: its right branch has height 0 and its left branch is empty (height −1), so bf = 0 − (−1) = +1.
Node 30: its right branch has height 1 and its left branch has height 2, so bf = 1 − 2 = −1.
Every balance factor is −1, 0 or +1, so this is an AVL tree, even though its levels are not full.

screens.title: Balanced does not mean full
screens.caption: Left: an AVL tree, although its levels are not full. Right: not an AVL tree, because node 7 has balance factor −2. These are the two trees in Figure 4.29 of the textbook.
screens.text: Requiring equal heights at every node would be too rigid: only perfect trees with 2ᵏ − 1 nodes would pass. The AVL rule allows a difference of 1 and still keeps the height O(log n).

screens.title: Summary
points: Height counts edges: a leaf has height 0, an empty branch −1.
bf = h(right) − h(left): negative means the left branch is taller.
AVL rule: every node has bf −1, 0 or +1, not only the root.
